records.reason: m94 at 20/1 and 50 uL completes a loading contrast with existing 100 and 150 uL observations. Supplied V1/V2 predictions are 38.53/86.78 mL. This tests whether the model misses loading dependence within a steep beta-ketoester response.

m94 at 10/1 and 150 uL connects the selected 20/1 point to existing 5/1, 10/1, and 20/1 observations. The existing loading anchors make this pair useful for separating solvent response from loading effects.

m13 at 1/1 and 100 uL fills the stronger-eluent portion of a multi-carbonyl ester curve. Its supplied prediction is 6.65/20.91 mL; the label can distinguish early completion broadening from the much later response at weaker eluent.

Methoxyethyl acrylate m20 at 10/1 and 50 uL extends coverage beyond its measured 1/1 and 5/1 conditions. It tests transfer from simple acrylates to an additional ether acceptor without selecting on predicted volume alone.
m107 at 1/1 and 50 uL completes a loading comparison with existing 100 and 150 uL observations. This supplies a baseline for the methoxyethyl beta-ketoester family before its large response at 5/1.
m28 at 1/1 and 150 uL fills a ratio gap between pure EA and the measured 2/1 and 5/1 conditions. This tests where the acetoxybenzaldehyde completion tail begins to develop.
m28 at 10/1 and 100 uL supplies the intermediate loading between measured 50 and 150 uL anchors. Its supplied 43.81/83.09 mL prediction tests whether onset and completion interpolate differently.

m125 at 5/1, 50 uL, and 500 uL DCM loading solution enables a direct loading-solvent-volume comparison with the measured 300 uL condition. It can distinguish injection-volume effects from a scaffold-wide retention correction.

m125 at 1/1, 100 uL, and 300 uL DCM loading solution fills a loading gap within the smaller injection-volume series. The supplied 10.85/29.93 mL prediction tests whether the model averages across distinct completion responses.
Methoxybenzophenone m114 at 20/1 and 100 uL fills a loading gap between measured 50 and 150 uL conditions. This gives completion supervision in a family with substantial weak-eluent tails.
m114 at 5/1 and 50 uL pairs with the selected 20/1 condition and existing loading anchors. It tests whether the diaryl ketone completion response grows smoothly as the mobile phase weakens.

Hydroxy-methoxybenzaldehyde m117 at 50/1 and 50 uL completes a loading comparison with measured 100 and 150 uL conditions. It tests onset and completion separately without treating the anomalous endpoint ordering at another ratio as a physical transition.
m117 at 1/1 and 50 uL provides a stronger-eluent anchor for the selected 50/1 point. The pair helps separate donor-containing scaffold response from unexplained variation at intermediate ratios.
Naphthylethanol m205 at 1/1 and 150 uL fills the high-loading baseline before its steep 2/1-to-5/1 response. Existing lower-loading observations allow an endpoint-specific loading comparison.

Naphthylmethanol m206 in pure EA at 100 uL supplies a baseline between existing loading anchors. It helps distinguish primary-alcohol topology effects from the large retention response at weaker mobile phases.

m72 at 5/1, 50 uL, with PE loading provides an independent row at a previously measured condition. This helps assess variability and loading-solvent transfer in an enamine ester family with markedly different completion responses across ratios.

Ortho-nitrobenzaldehyde m198 at 20/1 and 150 uL completes a loading comparison between existing 50 and 100 uL anchors. It constrains nitrocarbonyl condition response without assuming a universal nitro correction.

Methylbenzyl alcohol m135 at 5/1 and 50 uL completes the loading series at an intermediate retention condition. This can distinguish loading-dependent onset shifts from completion broadening within an accessible primary alcohol.

Secondary alcohol m60 at 10/1 and 150 uL completes a loading comparison with measured 50 and 100 uL conditions. The supplied 38.86/58.36 mL prediction tests transfer of the observed donor-family response to higher loading.

Para-aminobenzonitrile m160 in pure EA at 100 uL supplies a stronger-eluent baseline. Comparison with measured 1/1, 2/1, and 5/1 conditions tests how combined donor and nitrile environments change condition slope.

Meta-aminobenzonitrile m161 at 1/1 and 150 uL completes a loading series and complements the selected para isomer. This tests positional environment effects while retaining measured same-scaffold condition anchors.

Methylquinoline m146 at 2/1 and 50 uL fills a lower-loading condition before its steep weak-eluent response. It tests whether basic heteroaromatic onset and completion slopes transfer across loading amounts.

Methyl benzoylformate m92 at 50/1, 100 uL, with EA loading provides another row at a measured tuple. Existing observations show appreciable endpoint variation, so this label helps distinguish reproducibility limits from systematic alpha-ketoester completion bias.

Dimethylbenzonitrile m130 at 20/1 and 100 uL fills an intermediate-ratio/loading gap. Recent contrasting errors at 1/1 and 50/1 make this useful for testing local nitrile response rather than an additive acceptor offset.

Ethyl methoxybenzoate m87 at 50/1 and 150 uL completes a loading comparison with measured 50 and 100 uL conditions. This neutral ether-plus-ester scaffold constrains transfer from more strongly interacting carbonyl families.

Methyl anthranilate m104 at 1/1 and 150 uL fills the high-loading baseline for an ortho-amino ester. It tests whether donor/acceptor proximity and loading explain its nonuniform response across ratios.

Naphthylacetate ester m98 at 1/1 and 100 uL fills the stronger-eluent region of an otherwise well-anchored curve. Its label provides an ordinary aromatic ester constraint against overcorrecting oxygen-rich completion tails.

Dimethyl acetylenedicarboxylate m91 at 5/1 and 100 uL adds a loading contrast to the recent completion failure at 50 uL. Its supplied 8.15/10.24 mL prediction tests whether compact multi-acceptor behavior remains distinct from beta-ketoesters.

m91 at 2/1 and 100 uL pairs with the selected 5/1 point at identical loading conditions. As an additional row at a measured tuple, it also helps assess variability before attributing endpoint changes to solvent ratio.

Naphthaldehyde m195 at 1/1 and 100 uL supplies a stronger-eluent anchor for a family with good recent intermediate-ratio predictions but variable weaker-eluent onset. This constrains where tail corrections should apply.
Anisole m126 at 2/1 and 100 uL is a neutral single-acceptor control between existing loading anchors. It constrains spillover from corrections learned on donor-rich and multi-carbonyl compounds.

2,6-Dibromobenzaldehyde m184 at 2/1 and 100 uL supplies a sterically shielded, donor-free carbonyl control. Existing 50 and 150 uL observations make it useful for checking whether loading corrections transfer to simpler aromatic aldehydes.

hypotheses.content: Oxygen-rich carbonyl scaffolds require topology-specific PE/EA response curves; acceptor count alone does not explain onset and completion.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: The selected acrylate, beta-ketoester, aromatic aldehyde, amino ester, and neutral methoxybenzoate conditions teach which oxygen-containing environments share response shapes and which need separate calibration.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: At matched loading, do additional oxygen atoms alter both endpoints smoothly, or primarily change completion over particular solvent-ratio ranges?

hypotheses.content: Alcohol and phenolic donor responses depend strongly on scaffold and condition, and onset changes need not track completion changes.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: The alcohol and hydroxy-aldehyde selections add loading and solvent-response supervision across benzylic, nonbenzylic, fused aromatic, and phenolic environments.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: How much donor-family response transfers across topology after accounting for loading, and which endpoint retains a scaffold-specific difference?

hypotheses.content: Completion requires direct local calibration: historical V2 errors occur in both directions and cannot be repaired reliably through a universal shift or by inferring V2 from V1.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: Carbonyl completion points and a few repeated condition tuples provide supervision for endpoint decoupling while helping distinguish systematic bias from unexplained label variability.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Which completion differences are reproducible condition effects, and which reflect variation that the recorded features cannot explain?

hypotheses.content: Some apparent loading and loading-solvent-volume effects are scaffold- and endpoint-specific, while the supplied predictions are nearly invariant to loading in many matched candidate groups. Their reproducibility remains unresolved.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: The m94, m107, m28, and m125 selections complete useful loading comparisons; the m125 injection-volume contrast tests a recorded variable that may otherwise be averaged away.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do new matched labels reproduce the apparent loading or injection-volume dependence, and does that dependence affect onset, completion, or both?

hypotheses.content: Nitrile, amino, nitrocarbonyl, and basic heteroaromatic environments require context-specific condition slopes rather than a common strong-acceptor correction.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: The amino-nitrile isomers, simple aromatic nitrile, methylquinoline, and nitrobenzaldehyde conditions distinguish donor/acceptor combinations and basicity from a generic polarity effect.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Can the model transfer solvent-response shape across related acceptor environments while preserving the substantial differences between scaffolds?

feedback_interpretation: Recent feedback supports local endpoint calibration: substantial completion errors coexist with accurate ordinary carbonyl and ester predictions, so a global retention correction is inappropriate. The recent diethyl malonate and conjugated ketone outcomes also show that selecting only chemically unusual structures would miss useful failure regions. I weaken the earlier claim of a physical acid regime transition because near-zero negative completion and reversed endpoint labels do not establish such a mechanism. Repeated condition tuples show unexplained variability, so loading effects remain hypotheses rather than established causes. I use the catalog assignments and solvent convention consistently: m125 is dimethoxybenzaldehyde, m87 is a methoxybenzoate ester, 0/1 is pure EA, and increasing PE/EA weakens the mobile phase.
batch_rationale: This batch combines response-curve completion with targeted endpoint repair. Several measurements fill loading gaps between existing anchors, making them more interpretable than isolated high-retention points. The m125 loading-solvent-volume comparison tests a potentially underused recorded feature, while the m91 ratio pair tests solvent response at fixed loading. Amino-nitrile isomers and methylquinoline probe transfer across strong-interaction environments; donor-containing compounds test scaffold-sensitive onset and completion. Additional rows at a few measured tuples help assess reproducibility, and anisole, a shielded aromatic aldehyde, and ordinary aromatic esters constrain overcorrection. These labels may improve overall Row-distribution accuracy by refining structure-condition interactions and endpoint-specific response shapes. Quantile widths are treated as descriptive single-predictor outputs, not calibrated epistemic uncertainty.
